description: One compact Toki Pona word each week, a tiny sentence, and the much less tiny route by which its sound arrived.
weather: Meaning broad, grammar light, context doing most of the lifting.

entries.lede: The language’s own name begins in Tok Pisin tok and ultimately English talk, then expands to cover speech, language, conversation, and greeting.

origin.note: Toki is borrowed from Tok Pisin tok, ‘word’ or ‘speech’, itself from English talk.

sentence.note: Toki Pona content words are flexible. Here toki works as a greeting; elsewhere it can name speech or act as ‘speak’.

entries.weather: A warm front of meanings; expect context throughout the day.
entries.source_note: The immediate donor and the donor’s own source are kept separate. Toki Pona’s current meaning range is not limited to the donor word’s range.

entries.lede: Esperanto bona changes one consonant and becomes Toki Pona’s famously broad word for goodness, usefulness, simplicity, and improvement.

origin.note: Pona is borrowed from Esperanto bona, ‘good’. The shift b → p fits Toki Pona’s sound inventory.

sentence.note: After a third-person subject, li separates the subject from its predicate.

entries.source_note: The etymology identifies a source form; it does not restrict pona to the narrower job of a European adjective.

entries.lede: A Cantonese word for person passes almost intact into Toki Pona, where jan can be a person, people in general, or a personifying head noun.

origin.note: Jan is borrowed from Cantonese 人, romanised jan4 in Jyutping, meaning ‘person’. Toki Pona j is pronounced like English y.

sentence.note: Kama covers coming or becoming; context decides how much English machinery the translation needs.

entries.source_note: Tone is not carried into Toki Pona, which has no lexical tone. The sound shape is adapted to a much smaller phonological system.

entries.lede: A Japanese munching sound becomes Toki Pona’s general-purpose word for food and consumption—including drinking.

origin.note: Moku is associated with Japanese mogu mogu, an expressive form for chewing or munching, simplified into Toki Pona phonology.
comparisons: Japanese もぐもぐ mogu mogu

sentence.note: After mi, no li is used. The particle e marks the direct object kili.

entries.source_note: Expressive source forms do not map like formal dictionary equations. The modern Toki Pona word has a stable, broader grammatical life of its own.

entries.lede: Finnish suuri, ‘big’, is trimmed to Toki Pona’s phonology and grows semantically to cover size, importance, maturity, and length.

origin.note: Suli is borrowed from Finnish suuri, ‘big’ or ‘large’; Toki Pona lacks r, so the adapted form uses l.

sentence.note: Modifiers follow their head: suli describes ma. The same phrase might be understood as a country, continent, or simply large area.

entries.source_note: The sound adaptation is documented; the generous modern semantic range comes from Toki Pona usage and context.

entries.lede: Tok Pisin liklik loses its final consonants but keeps its reduplicated rhythm, becoming the compact opposite of suli.

origin.note: Lili comes from Tok Pisin liklik, ‘small’ or ‘a little’, adapted to Toki Pona’s open syllables.

sentence.note: Lon can mean existing, present, at, or in. The English location word is supplied by context.

entries.source_note: The immediate model is Tok Pisin, even though that language’s word has an English history of its own.

entries.lede: Acadian French de l’eau is heard as a compact two-syllable form and becomes Toki Pona’s broad word for liquids.

origin.note: Telo is traced to Acadian French de l’eau, ‘of/from the water’, reshaped to fit Toki Pona’s sound pattern.

sentence.note: Moku covers consuming both food and drink. Telo can be water specifically or liquid more generally.

entries.source_note: The route is a reminder that borrowing follows heard phrases, accents, and communities—not just dictionary headwords.

entries.lede: Esperanto suno makes the trip into Toki Pona unchanged in spelling, then widens from the sun itself to light and shining.

origin.note: Toki Pona borrowed suno directly from Esperanto suno, ‘sun’. Both languages pronounce it with first-syllable stress.

sentence.note: Seli covers heat, fire, cooking, and warmth. A small lexicon lets related ideas share a word.

entries.source_note: This is a borrowing chain visible across the three gardens: English influenced Esperanto suno, which directly supplied Toki Pona suno.

entries.lede: Finnish kasvi sheds one consonant and becomes a broad Toki Pona category for growing green things and their plant-like products.

origin.note: Kasi is borrowed from Finnish kasvi, ‘plant’, with the consonant cluster simplified.

sentence.note: Laso covers a colour region that includes both green and blue; the plant makes the intended reading unsurprising.

entries.source_note: Borrowed sounds are simplified, while the meaning is organised by Toki Pona’s own deliberately broad categories.

entries.lede: Dutch hagedis, ‘lizard’, is radically smoothed into akesi and grows into a category whose emotional boundary is famously context-sensitive.

origin.note: Akesi is borrowed from Dutch hagedis, ‘lizard’, with consonants and syllables adapted to Toki Pona’s inventory.

sentence.translation: A reptile is beside the water.
sentence.note: Poka literally concerns side or proximity; lon poka telo supplies the location phrase.

entries.source_note: Older glosses sometimes overemphasise ‘non-cute’. Actual categorisation varies, so the page lists the zoological centre before the cultural joke.

entries.lede: A Georgian animal word is re-cut into Toki Pona syllables and becomes the usual category for furry land animals.

origin.note: Soweli is traced to Georgian ცხოველი (cxoveli), ‘animal’, substantially adapted to Toki Pona phonology.

sentence.note: Lape can be sleep or rest. No tense marking forces the translation to be present; context normally handles time.

entries.source_note: The visual difference between source and result is a useful lesson: borrowing can preserve a recognisable rhythm without preserving every segment.

entries.lede: French oiseau is heard and simplified into waso, a category happy to extend beyond strict ornithology when context wants wings.

origin.note: Waso is borrowed from French oiseau, ‘bird’, with the initial glide and vowels adapted into two open syllables.

sentence.translation: The bird moves in the sky.
sentence.note: Sewi covers high, above, sky, and sacredness. Here the location selects the sky reading.

entries.source_note: The etymology records the sound source. The present category is defined by Toki Pona speakers and the needs of each phrase.

entries.lede: Kili groups fruit, vegetables and mushrooms together. A shopping basket can be more useful than a botanical boundary.

origin.note: Linku records Georgian ხილი (xili), meaning fruit, as the donor.

sentence.note: Ni follows the noun it specifies. Jelo is the predicate after li; this context selects the fruit reading of kili.

entries.source_note: Linku reproduces the pu definition and separately records the Georgian origin. The wider food category belongs to Toki Pona usage, not to an expanded translation of the donor.

sources.title: Linku: kili, pu definition and documented origin

entries.lede: Luka can name the hand or count five. The sentence has to tell you which job it is doing.

origin.note: Linku records Serbo-Croatian ruka, hand or arm, as the donor. The adapted Toki Pona form has l where the donor has r.

sentence.note: Mi follows luka as a possessor. Toki Pona leaves number unmarked here, so a singular hand or an arm could also fit another context.

entries.source_note: The pu definition reported by Linku includes the bodily sense and the numeral five. The example chooses a bodily reading without turning five into part of the donor’s gloss.

sources.title: Linku: luka, bodily and numerical senses and origin

entries.lede: A nasin can be a route across town or a way of doing something. This week’s example stays on the road.

origin.note: Linku identifies Serbo-Croatian način, way or method, as the source. Its č is adapted as s in nasin.

sentence.note: Literally, this way is big. Wide is a contextual English reading of suli with a road; nasin ni is an ordinary phrase, not a fixed compound.

entries.source_note: The donor explains the sound source, while Linku’s pu definition covers both physical routes and methods. No literal-road restriction follows from the etymology.

sources.title: Linku: nasin, pu definition and Serbo-Croatian origin

entries.lede: Lape makes room for a pause. In this sentence, resting is enough; falling asleep is optional.

origin.note: Linku records Dutch slapen, to sleep, as the donor. Toki Pona lape also covers resting, so its present range is broader than this one donor gloss.

sentence.note: With mi alone as the subject, there is no li before the predicate. The same clause can describe sleeping when the situation calls for that reading.

entries.source_note: Linku reports the sleeping and resting senses from pu and identifies the Dutch source separately. The example does not add tense: present time is an English choice supplied by context.

sources.title: Linku: lape, pu definition and Dutch origin

entries.lede: Kiwen can be a stone in the path or a piece of metal. Hardness gives the word its useful breadth.

origin.note: The documented donor is Finnish kiven, the genitive form of the word for stone. That borrowed sound shape does not make kiwen a genitive form in Toki Pona.

sentence.note: Ni follows the object it identifies, and li introduces the predicate suli. Stone is the contextual reading of kiwen; another setting could make it a different hard object.

entries.source_note: Linku explicitly names the Finnish genitive donor and reproduces the pu range covering hard objects, stone and metal. Kiwen ni is an ordinary descriptive phrase, not a separate dictionary compound.

sources.title: Linku: kiwen, material senses and Finnish genitive donor

entries.lede: The spelling looks familiar to an English reader, and this time the borrowing record agrees. The vowels still follow Toki Pona pronunciation.

origin.note: Linku identifies English open as the donor. The Toki Pona word also covers beginning an activity or turning something on.

sentence.note: The particle e introduces poki as the direct object. Mi takes no li here; this example uses open as the main predicate.

entries.source_note: The donor is documented, not inferred from identical spelling. Linku’s pu definition supports the opening sense used here; no fixed compound or special preverb construction is needed.

sources.title: Linku: open, pu meanings and English donor
